scenarios.prompt: One shoulder blade lifts a little from the ribs as a client lowers from overhead; no pain, no warning signs.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Continue with a load and range they control; note it; no referral without warning signs.

scenarios.prompt: Same client, but the shoulder aches more with each rep.
scenarios.goodAnswer: Stop shoulder loading for this session. If the pain is getting worse: routine referral now (GP or physiotherapist). If it has not improved after 2 weeks: routine referral. Urgent or emergency if those signs appear.

lesson.title: Scapulohumeral rhythm
lesson.summary: When the arm goes up, the shoulder blade moves with it. Learn what that shared movement looks like and how to watch it.
objectives: Describe the shoulder blade movements that happen as the arm is raised.
Explain that raising the arm is shared with the shoulder blade, and that the share varies between people.
Watch a client raise their arms and describe what you see in plain words.
Explain why a visible difference in shoulder blade movement is something to watch and re-check, not a diagnosis.

blocks.content: Raise your arm overhead and the shoulder blade comes along. Watching that shared movement is a useful coaching skill, as long as you remember what it can and cannot tell you.

When the arm is raised, the shoulder blade does not stay still. In people without shoulder pain, from the very start of the raise it rotates upward, so the socket turns to face more toward the ceiling, and it tilts backward. It also tends to turn outward around the ribcage.

content.alt: Three schematic drawings of a right shoulder blade seen from behind, in a person without shoulder pain, with the arm by the side, level with the shoulder and overhead. The shoulder blade is rotated upward more at each position.
content.caption: The shoulder blade at three arm positions in a person without shoulder pain, right shoulder blade seen from behind. Schematic; angles are illustrative.

legend.label: Arm level with the shoulder.
legend.text: The shoulder blade has rotated upward.

blocks.content: Raising the arm is shared with the shoulder blade. A review that pooled studies of people without shoulder pain estimated that the arm rises about three degrees for every degree the shoulder blade rotates upward. Shoulder blade movement varied a lot between people, and the review did not support a fixed ratio.
Do not count degrees on the gym floor. Watch whether the arm and the shoulder blade move together.

Changes in how the shoulder blade moves, often called scapular dyskinesis, are present in a high percentage of shoulder injuries. An international consensus statement concluded that their exact role in causing or worsening shoulder problems is not clearly defined.
So treat a visible difference as something to watch and re-check, not as a diagnosis. It never tells you on its own what is wrong, or that nothing is.

content: Stand behind the client. Ask first; a fitted top lets you see the shoulder blades without asking anyone to undress.
Ask them to raise both arms slowly forward and up, then lower them, 3 to 5 times.
Watch both shoulder blades: do they start moving at a similar time and travel a similar amount?
On the way down, watch the inner edge and the bottom tip of each shoulder blade. Do they stay close to the ribs or lift away?
If differences are hard to see, a light dumbbell in each hand can make them clearer.
Write down what you saw in plain words, for example: "left shoulder blade lifts away from the ribs on the way down."

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: If pain comes on or rises, or any warning sign appears: Stop shoulder loading for the rest of the session. Pain that is getting worse: routine referral now; do not wait. Pain that has not improved after 2 weeks: routine referral. Pins and needles that do not go away, or no feeling in the arm or shoulder: urgent, today. A new inability to lift or move the arm themselves, without an injury: urgent, today. After a fall or impact, an arm they cannot move or a shoulder that looks out of place: emergency, now. Do not move the arm or try to put it back. This never clears anyone and never names an injury. The full stop rules and referral tiers are in "When to refer out" (lesson 8).

blocks.content: What to do: cues for overhead work

"Shoulder blades back and down" is a common cue, and it helps some lifters set up for a bench press. Overhead, the same cue can fight the upward rotation described above. For overhead reaching, try "reach long through your hands" or "let your shoulder blades travel with your arms".
Give one cue, watch the next rep, and keep the cue only if the movement changes the way you want. If it does not, drop it and try a different position or a lighter load.

content.prompt: In people without shoulder pain, which two shoulder blade movements happen as the arm is raised overhead?
options: None: the shoulder blade stays still
content.explanation: In people without shoulder pain, from the start of the raise the shoulder blade rotates upward and tilts backward, and it tends to turn outward around the ribcage.

content.prompt: How is raising the arm shared with the shoulder blade?
options: On average about three degrees of arm rise per degree of shoulder blade rotation, with large differences between people
The shoulder blade does most of the work
content.explanation: Pooled studies of people without shoulder pain estimated about 3:1 on average; shoulder blade movement varied a lot between people, and the review did not support a fixed ratio.

content.prompt: What did an international consensus statement conclude about scapular dyskinesis?
options: It is present in a high percentage of shoulder injuries, but its exact role in causing or worsening them is not clearly defined
It is never seen with shoulder injuries
content.explanation: It is common in shoulder injuries, but its exact role in causing or worsening shoulder problems is not clearly defined.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: One shoulder blade lifts a little from the ribs as a client lowers from overhead. They have no pain and no other warning signs. Do you continue, adjust or refer? Now change one thing: the shoulder aches more with each rep. What do you do first, and what happens next?
